title: Diode Models & Load Lines
description: Find diode operating points graphically with load lines, or quickly with ideal, constant-drop and piecewise-linear models.

study.title: Load-line analysis
study.body: For a source $V_{SS}$, a resistor $R$ and a diode in series, KVL gives a straight line in the $i_D$–$v_D$ plane: the **load line**. It meets the axes at $v_D = V_{SS}$ (where $i_D = 0$) and at $i_D = V_{SS}/R$ (where $v_D = 0$). The **operating point** (Q point) is where the load line crosses the diode characteristic. Drag $V_{SS}$: the line moves parallel to itself. Drag $R$: it rotates about the point $(V_{SS}, 0)$. Either way the Q point slides along the steep diode curve, so $V_{DQ}$ hardly changes while $I_{DQ}$ changes a lot.

study.title: Load lines for larger circuits
study.body: If a circuit has resistors, sources and a **single** nonlinear element, first replace the linear part by its Thévenin equivalent $V_t$, $R_t$. Then the load line is $V_t = R_t i_D + v_D$. Its slope is $-1/R_t$: changing the source shifts the line parallel to itself; changing the resistance rotates it about $(V_t, 0)$.

study.title: Ideal-diode model
study.body:
The ideal diode is a perfect one-way switch.
- **On:** short circuit, $v_D = 0$; valid if $i_D > 0$.
- **Off:** open circuit, $i_D = 0$; valid if $v_D < 0$.
It works well when the circuit voltages are much larger than the 0.7 V diode drop.

study.title: Assumed-states analysis
study.body:
- Assume a state (on or off) for every diode.
- Replace on-diodes by their on-model and off-diodes by open circuits; solve the linear circuit.
- Check: on-diodes need $i_D > 0$ (forward), off-diodes need $v_D$ below the turn-on voltage.
- If a check fails, change that assumption and solve again.
Tip: if two diodes in an assumed state would force a node to two different voltages, that state is impossible.

study.title: Constant-voltage-drop model
study.body: A conducting diode is replaced by a 0.7 V source (+ at the anode); an off diode by an open circuit. On is valid if $i_D > 0$; off is valid if $v_D < 0.7$ V. For the simple series circuit:

study.title: Piecewise-linear models
study.body: Approximate the characteristic by straight-line segments. A forward segment through $(v_1, i_1)$ and $(v_2, i_2)$ becomes a source $V_a$ in series with a resistance $R_a = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{i_2 - i_1}$, where $V_a$ is where the line crosses $i_D = 0$. The ideal and constant-drop models are the special cases with $R_a = 0$.

steps.title: Writing the load line
steps.body: The diode equation is nonlinear, so we solve graphically. KVL around the loop gives a **straight line** relating $i_D$ and $v_D$, set only by the linear part of the circuit.

steps.prompt: With $V_{SS}$ = {{VSS|V}} and $R$ = {{R|Ω}}, where does the load line cross the $i_D$ axis (the point with $v_D = 0$)?
steps.explanation: Set $v_D = 0$ in $V_{SS} = Ri_D + v_D$: $i_D = V_{SS}/R$ = {{VSS}} V / {{R|Ω}} = {{VSS/R|A}}.

steps.prompt: Where does the same load line cross the $v_D$ axis (the point with $i_D = 0$)?
steps.explanation: With $i_D = 0$ there is no drop across $R$, so $v_D = V_{SS}$. The two intercepts $(V_{SS}, 0)$ and $(0, V_{SS}/R)$ are enough to draw the line.

steps.title: The operating point
steps.body: The diode must satisfy both its own characteristic and the load line, so the **operating point** (Q point) is their intersection. Because the forward characteristic is so steep, the Q point of a conducting silicon diode usually sits at $v_D \approx$ 0.6–0.7 V.

steps.prompt: In the series circuit of a source, a resistor and a forward diode, $V_{SS}$ = {{VSS|V}} and $R$ = {{R|Ω}}. The load line crosses the diode characteristic at $v_D$ = {{vQ|V}}. Find $i_D$ at the Q point.
steps.explanation: The Q point lies on the load line: $i_D = \frac{V_{SS} - v_D}{R} = \frac{ {{VSS}} - {{vQ}} }{ {{R}} }$ = {{(VSS-vQ)/R|A}}.

steps.prompt: Increasing $V_{SS}$ while keeping $R$ fixed shifts the load line parallel to itself.
steps.explanation: The slope of the load line is $-1/R$, which does not depend on $V_{SS}$. Both intercepts grow in proportion, so the line moves parallel to itself.

steps.prompt: What happens to the load line if $R$ is increased while $V_{SS}$ stays the same?
options: It rotates about $(V_{SS}, 0)$ and becomes flatter
It shifts parallel to the right
steps.explanation: The $v_D$-intercept $V_{SS}$ stays put, while the $i_D$-intercept $V_{SS}/R$ drops. So the line rotates about $(V_{SS}, 0)$ and gets a flatter slope $-1/R$: the Q-point current decreases.

steps.title: Try it: moving the load line
steps.body: Drag the sliders. A larger $V_{SS}$ shifts the load line to the right without changing its slope $-1/R$; a larger $R$ makes it flatter. Watch the readouts: the current follows the circuit, but the diode voltage stays near 0.7 V. That is why the constant-voltage-drop model works so well.

steps.prompt: To draw a load line for this diode, first find the Thévenin voltage $V_t$ seen by the diode (the $v_D$-intercept of the load line).
steps.explanation:
Remove the diode and find the open-circuit voltage across its terminals with the divider:
$V_t = V_s\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = {{Vs}}\times\frac{ {{R2}} }{ {{R1}} + {{R2}} }$ = {{Vs*R2/(R1+R2)|V}}.
(The Thévenin resistance is $R_1 \| R_2$ = {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}}, so the load line is $V_t = R_t i_D + v_D$.)

steps.title: Quick models
steps.body:
- **Ideal diode:** on = short ($v_D = 0$, needs $i_D > 0$), off = open ($i_D = 0$, needs $v_D < 0$).
- **Constant-voltage drop:** on = 0.7 V source ($i_D > 0$), off = open ($v_D < 0.7$ V).
Assume a state, solve, then check the assumption.

steps.prompt: Using the **ideal-diode** model, find $i_D$.
steps.explanation:
Assume D is on (short circuit). Then all of $V_{SS}$ is across $R$:
$i_D = V_{SS}/R$ = {{VSS}} V / {{R|Ω}} = {{VSS/R|A}}.
Check: $i_D > 0$, so the assumption holds.

steps.prompt: Using the ideal-diode model, find $v_D$ (referenced + at the anode) and $i_D$.
steps.explanation:
The cathode faces the + terminal, so assume D is off (open). Then $i_D = 0$, there is no drop across $R$, the cathode is at {{VSS|V}} and the anode at 0 V: $v_D$ = 0 − {{VSS}} = {{-VSS|V}}.
Check: $v_D < 0$, so off is correct. (Assuming on would give a negative $i_D$.)

steps.prompt: Now use the **constant-voltage-drop** model with 0.7 V. Find $i_D$.
steps.explanation:
Assume D is on and replace it by a 0.7 V source:
$i_D = \frac{V_{SS} - 0.7}{R} = \frac{ {{VSS}} - 0.7}{ {{R}} }$ = {{(VSS-0.7)/R|A}}.
Check: $i_D > 0$. The ideal model would give {{VSS/R|A}}; the difference matters most for small $V_{SS}$.

steps.prompt: Using the 0.7 V constant-drop model for both diodes, find the loop current $i$.
steps.explanation:
Both diodes point the same way around the loop, so assume both on. KVL: $V_{SS} = Ri + 0.7 + 0.7$, so
$i = \frac{ {{VSS}} - 1.4}{ {{R}} }$ = {{(VSS-1.4)/R|A}}.
The result is positive, so both diodes are indeed on.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of assumed-states analysis in order
items: Assume a state (on or off) for each diode
Replace on-diodes by their on-model and off-diodes by open circuits
Check $i_D > 0$ for on-diodes and $v_D$ below turn-on for off-diodes
If a check fails, change that assumption and repeat
steps.explanation: Guess, solve, check. Each diode model is linear once the state is fixed, so the circuit can be solved with ordinary circuit analysis. The checks tell you whether the guess was consistent.

steps.prompt: Using the 0.7 V model, find the diode current $i_D$ (anode to cathode).
steps.explanation:
Assume D on. KVL around the loop: $V_{in} = Ri_D + 0.7 + V_B$, so
$i_D = \frac{ {{Vin}} - 0.7 - {{VB}} }{ {{R}} }$ = {{(Vin-VB-0.7)/R|A}}.
$i_D > 0$, so the assumption is consistent. The diode only conducts when $V_{in} > V_B + 0.7$ V.

steps.prompt: In ideal-diode analysis, if a diode assumed **on** turns out to have a negative $i_D$, the assumption was wrong.
steps.explanation: An ideal diode can only conduct in the forward direction, so an on-diode must have $i_D > 0$. A negative result means the diode is actually off: redo the analysis with it as an open circuit.

steps.prompt: Using the 0.7 V model, find the diode current $i_D$. (Hint: replace $V_s$, $R_1$, $R_2$ by a Thévenin equivalent first.)
steps.explanation:
Thévenin equivalent to the left of D:
$V_t = {{Vs}}\frac{ {{R2}} }{ {{R1}} + {{R2}} }$ = {{Vt|V}}, $R_t = R_1\|R_2$ = {{Rt|Ω}}.
Assume D on: $i_D = \frac{V_t - 0.7}{R_t + R_3} = \frac{ {{Vt}} - 0.7}{ {{Rt}} + {{R3}} }$ = {{iD|A}} (positive, so D is on).

steps.prompt: The inputs are held at $V_A$ = {{VA|V}} and $V_B$ = {{VB|V}} relative to ground. Using the 0.7 V model, which diodes conduct?
steps.explanation:
Both on is impossible: $v_o$ would have to be {{VA-0.7}} V and {{VB-0.7}} V at the same time.
Assume only $D_A$ on: $v_o = V_A - 0.7$ = {{VA-0.7|V}}, and $i_{DA} = v_o/R > 0$ ✓. For $D_B$: $v_D = V_B - v_o$ = {{VB-VA+0.7|V}} < 0.7 V ✓, so $D_B$ is off. The higher input wins: this is a diode OR gate.

steps.prompt: Diode logic gate, 0.7 V model. The inputs are $V_A$ = 5 V, $V_B$ = 0 V and $V_C$ = 5 V. Tap every diode that **conducts**.
steps.explanation:
The resistor pulls current from +5 V into the anodes. The diode with the **lowest** cathode voltage takes it: $D_B$ conducts and clamps
$$v_o = V_B + 0.7 = 0.7\text{ V}$$
Now $D_A$ and $D_C$ have 0.7 V on the anode and 5 V on the cathode: reverse biased, off. (Check: if $D_A$ were on, $v_o$ would be 5.7 V and $D_B$ would have 5.7 V across it, impossible.) This circuit is an AND gate: $v_o$ is high only if all inputs are high.

steps.prompt: In the same diode OR circuit, $V_A$ = {{VA|V}}, $V_B$ = {{VB|V}} and $R$ = {{R|Ω}}. Using the 0.7 V model, find $v_o$.
steps.explanation:
The diode at the higher input conducts and the other is reverse biased. Here $D_B$ is on: $v_o = V_B - 0.7$ = {{max(VA,VB)-0.7|V}}.
Check $D_A$: $v_D = V_A - v_o$ = {{VA-VB+0.7|V}} < 0.7 V, so it is off.

steps.prompt: Using the 0.7 V model, find the node voltage $v_A$ (top of $R_2$, relative to ground).
A piecewise-linear diode model uses the straight line through ({{v1|V}}, {{i1|A}}) and ({{v1+dv|V}}, {{i1+di|A}}). Find the series resistance $R_a$ of the model.
steps.explanation:
$R_a$ is the inverse slope of the line:
$R_a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta i} = \frac{ {{dv}}\text{ V} }{ {{di}}\text{ A} }$ = {{dv/di|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: For the line through ({{v1|V}}, {{i1|A}}) and ({{v1+dv|V}}, {{i1+di|A}}), find the model voltage $V_a$, where the line crosses $i_D = 0$.
steps.explanation:
$R_a = \Delta v/\Delta i$ = {{Ra|Ω}}. On the line $v_D = V_a + R_a i_D$, so using the first point:
$V_a = v_1 - R_a i_1 = {{v1}} - {{Ra}}\times{{i1}}$ = {{Va|V}}.

steps.prompt: A diode is modeled by $V_a$ = {{Va|V}} in series with $R_a$ = {{Ra|Ω}} when on. It is in series with $R$ = {{R|Ω}} across $V_{SS}$ = {{VSS|V}} (forward direction). Find $i_D$.
steps.explanation:
Replace the diode by its model: $V_{SS} = (R + R_a)i_D + V_a$, so
$i_D = \frac{ {{VSS}} - {{Va}} }{ {{R}} + {{Ra}} }$ = {{(VSS-Va)/(R+Ra)|A}}.
Then $v_D = V_a + R_a i_D$ = {{Va+Ra*(VSS-Va)/(R+Ra)|V}}.

steps.prompt: Match each diode model with its equivalent circuit
steps.explanation: All three on-models are linear: a short, a fixed voltage source, or a source with a series resistance. In every model an off diode is an open circuit.

steps.prompt: A source $V_{SS}$, a resistor $R$ and a diode are connected in series. The graph shows the diode characteristic (green) and the load line of the circuit (orange). Read the diode current at the operating point.
steps.explanation: The operating point (Q point) is where the load line crosses the diode curve, because both equations must hold at once. Going left from the crossing to the $i_D$ axis gives $i_D$ ≈ {{iQ|A}}, at $v_D$ ≈ {{vQ||2}} V. Check with KVL: $i_D = (V_{SS} - v_D)/R$ = ({{VSS|V}} − {{vQ||2}} V) / {{R|Ω}} = {{iQ|A}}.

steps.prompt: The orange line is the load line of a series circuit with a source $V_{SS}$, a resistor $R$ and the diode. Read the intercepts of the load line and find $R$.
steps.explanation: The load line $V_{SS} = R\,i_D + v_D$ meets the $v_D$ axis at $v_D = V_{SS}$ = {{VSS|V}} (there $i_D$ = 0) and the $i_D$ axis at $i_D = V_{SS}/R$ = {{isc|A}} (there $v_D$ = 0). So $R$ = {{VSS|V}} / {{isc|A}} = {{R|Ω}}. Its slope is $-1/R$.

steps.prompt: One component value of the diode circuit was changed, which moved the load line from the solid orange line (before) to the dashed blue line (after). What was changed?
steps.explanation:
The load line runs from $(V_{SS}, 0)$ on the $v_D$ axis to $(0, V_{SS}/R)$ on the $i_D$ axis, with slope $-1/R$.
- Only $V_{SS}$ changed: same slope, the line **shifts parallel** (right for a larger $V_{SS}$).
- Only $R$ changed: same $v_D$ intercept, the line **rotates** about $(V_{SS}, 0)$: flatter for a larger $R$, steeper for a smaller $R$.

steps.prompt: The graph shows a piecewise-linear diode model: no current below $V_a$, and $v_D = V_a + R_a i_D$ when the diode conducts.

ask.explanation: $V_a$ is where the sloped segment meets $i_D$ = 0: the line leaves the axis at $v_D$ ≈ {{Va|V}}. In the circuit model it is a voltage source of {{Va|V}} in series with $R_a$.

ask.prompt: Find $R_a$ from the slope of the conducting segment.
ask.explanation: Take two points on the sloped segment: it starts at $V_a$ = {{Va|V}} with $i_D$ = 0 and reaches {{(1.4-Va)/Ra|A}} at $v_D$ = 1.4 V. $R_a = \Delta v_D/\Delta i_D$ = (1.4 V − {{Va|V}}) / {{(1.4-Va)/Ra|A}} = {{Ra|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Which graph shows the **constant-voltage-drop** model of a diode? ($v_D$ horizontal, $i_D$ vertical, gridlines every 0.5 V.)
steps.explanation: The constant-voltage-drop model says: no current below 0.7 V, and any current at exactly 0.7 V. Its graph is the $v_D$ axis up to 0.7 V and then a **vertical** line at 0.7 V. A vertical line at 0 V is the ideal-diode model; a sloped line starting at $V_a$ is a piecewise-linear model with $R_a > 0$; a line through the origin is a plain resistor.

steps.prompt: In this circuit ($R$ = {{R|Ω}}) the diode follows the green characteristic. Set $V_{SS}$ so that the diode current is {{I|A}}.
steps.hint: Read $v_D$ at the wanted current from the diode curve; then KVL gives $V_{SS}$.
steps.explanation:
At $i_D$ = {{I|A}} the diode curve gives $v_D$ ≈ {{vI||3}} V (the Q point must lie on the characteristic). KVL around the loop:
$V_{SS} = R\,i_D + v_D$ = {{R|Ω}} × {{I|A}} + {{vI||3}} V = **{{Vt|V}}**.
The load line then runs from $(V_{SS}, 0)$ with slope $-1/R$ through that point.
